title: Infection Process and Normal Immune Response
introduction: Infection occurs when a disease-causing microorganism invades the body and overwhelms host-specific defences, producing localized or systemic responses[cite: 327]. Understanding the chain of infection, antimicrobial resistance, and the body's multi-layered normal immune system—spanning physical barriers, lymphoid organs, humoral immunity, and cell-mediated immunity—guides evidence-based infection control and clinical nursing care[cite: 333, 334, 358, 369].
learningOutcomes: 4.1 Define infection, distinguish communicable, nosocomial, and opportunistic infections, and outline the four stages of infection[cite: 327, 328, 329].
4.2 Trace the sequential links in the cycle of infection, classify infectious agents and their sources, and apply nursing interventions to break each link in the chain[cite: 329, 332, 333, 334].
4.3 Explain mechanisms and drivers of antibiotic resistance, patient teaching principles, gerontologic implications of infection, and emerging and re-emerging infections[cite: 334, 335, 336].
4.4 Define immunity, identify the four anatomical components of the immune system, and explain the five core properties of the immune response[cite: 357, 358, 364, 365].

4.5 Differentiate innate versus acquired immunity (active/passive, natural/artificial), antigens versus haptens, MHC classes I and II, humoral versus cell-mediated immunity, and the five antigen-antibody interactions[cite: 365, 366, 368, 369, 371].

content.heading: Concept, Types, Stages, and Cycle of Infection
content.body: Infection is the invasion of the body by a disease-causing microorganism (pathogen) with a resultant host response, occurring only when host-specific body defences are overwhelmed[cite: 327]. Infections fall into three main types: communicable diseases (transmitted from an infected person, animal, or object to an uninfected person), nosocomial infections (acquired within healthcare facilities such as hospitals and clinics), and opportunistic infections (occurring in immunocompromised hosts—such as older adults or organ transplant recipients—from microbes that rarely harm healthy hosts or from normal flora; Hargrove-Huttel, 2005)[cite: 328]. Every infection progresses through four stages: incubation (time from entry to symptom onset, when the host is often most infectious—e.g., varicella/chickenpox has a 2–3 week incubation and is contagious from 5 days before rash eruption), prodromal, illness, and convalescence[cite: 329]. For infection to occur, six sequential links must connect: (1) infectious agent (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites), (2) reservoir of infection (person, animal, plant, or location providing nourishment—commonly the urinary tract, respiratory tract, or surgical wounds in humans), (3) portal of exit (route leaving the host), (4) mode of transmission (direct/indirect contact via fomites or secretions, airborne droplet nuclei/dusts such as tuberculosis and histoplasmosis, or animate vectors such as mosquitoes, fleas, and lice), (5) portal of entry (skin via burrowing like hookworm larvae or integument breaks, GI tract via contaminated food/water like typhoid and hepatitis A, respiratory tract via droplets, genitourinary tract, or transplacental transmission like syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis B), and (6) susceptible host (vulnerability heightened by age, comorbidities, chronic stress, poor nutrition, lack of immunization, invasive procedures like catheterization, and immunosuppressive therapy)[cite: 329, 330, 331, 332].

content.heading: Infectious Agents, Sources, and Breaking the Chain of Infection
content.body: Exposure to pathogens can result in no infection, subclinical infection, self-limiting disease, or severe disease requiring treatment[cite: 332]. Biological agents include viruses (the smallest obligate intracellular pathogens), bacteria, fungi, and parasites—spanning helminths (cestodes/tapeworms, nematodes/roundworms, trematodes/flukes), protozoa (malaria, amoebic dysentery), arthropods (ticks, mosquitoes, biting flies), and human ectoparasites (scabies mites, lice, fleas)[cite: 332]. An organism's capacity to cause infection depends on virulence (ability to grow and multiply), invasiveness (ability to enter tissue), and pathogenicity (ability to cause disease)[cite: 333]. Sources include endogenous flora, exogenous environments (water, soil, food, air), congenital/vertical transmission, contaminated fomites (e.g., handkerchiefs), and animal zoonoses (cat-scratch disease, rabies, Lyme disease)[cite: 333]. Nurses disrupt the chain of infection at six points: (1) agent-to-reservoir via cleansing, disinfection, and sterilization; (2) reservoir-to-portal of exit via hygiene, aseptic dressing changes, equipment sterilization, clean/properly disposed linens, and covering coughs/sneezes; (3) portal of exit-to-transmission via hand hygiene, medical/surgical asepsis, proper contaminated waste disposal, gloves, masks, and goggles; (4) transmission-to-portal of entry via proper sharps disposal, sterile technique, gowning/gloving, and intact skin; (5) portal of entry-to-host via preserving skin integrity and preventing needlestick injuries; and (6) susceptible host-to-agent via good nutrition, immunization, exercise, intact immunity, and adequate rest[cite: 333, 334].

content.heading: Antibiotic Resistance, Gerontologic Implications, and Emerging Infections
content.body: Antibiotic resistance occurs when adaptable bacteria use genetic changes (mutations or acquiring new DNA) and biochemical mechanisms (drug-deactivating enzymes) to alter drug target sites so antibiotics cannot bind or enter (Lewis & Heitkemper, 2011)[cite: 334]. Resistance is accelerated by giving antibiotics for viral infections, prescribing unnecessary drugs under patient pressure, using inadequate/incomplete regimens, substituting broad-spectrum or combination agents when first-line drugs suffice, incomplete patient dosing, and limited resources[cite: 334]. Patient teaching stresses six habits: never take antibiotics to prevent illness, practice frequent hand washing (the single most important infection-prevention measure), avoid skipping doses, finish the full prescription even after symptoms resolve, do not request antibiotics for viral colds or flu, and never take leftover antibiotics[cite: 334]. In older adults, age-related declines in immunocompetency, comorbidities, and disability increase pneumonia, catheter-associated nosocomial UTIs, skin infections, and tuberculosis; importantly, elderly patients may show cognitive or behavioural changes as early signs and often lack fever due to lower core temperature and blunted immune responses[cite: 335]. Emerging infections (over 30 newly recognized in the past 20 years) include HIV, Lyme disease, hepatitis C, SARS (linked to civet cats), West Nile virus (mosquitoes), avian flu (spreading from chickens to humans in Hong Kong in 1997 and the Netherlands in 2003), and Ebola virus (whose natural reservoir and transmission path remain unknown)[cite: 335]. Re-emerging infections include tuberculosis (rising since 1984 due to HIV, public health funding cuts, and multidrug-resistant MDR-TB) and measles (driven by travel to endemic regions)[cite: 336].

content.heading: Normal Immunity: Definition, Anatomical Components, and Properties
content.body: Immunity is the state of responsiveness to foreign substances—the body's ability to distinguish 'self' from 'nonself' (antigens) to perform three core functions: defence (destroying microbes; hyper-response causes allergies, hypo-response causes immunodeficiency), homeostasis (clearing damaged cells; hyper-response causes autoimmune disease), and surveillance (eliminating mutated cells; hypo-response leads to malignancy)[cite: 357, 368]. The immune system comprises four anatomical components[cite: 358]: (1) Physical barriers—intact keratinized skin with acidic pH, salty sweat, sebum, and epidermal Langerhans' cells (whose depletion prevents skin-localized delayed hypersensitivity); respiratory nasal hairs, IgA-rich mucus, cilia moving debris to the carina to trigger coughing, and lung Surfactants A and D that coat pathogens for phagocytosis; digestive defences including slightly acidic saliva (with IgA, bactericidal lysozymes, and cytokine-like defensins), gastric HCl and pepsin, intestinal bile salts/enzymes, and protective large-intestine flora; ocular eyelashes, blinking, and IgA-containing tears; and vaginal lactobacilli producing protective lactic acid[cite: 359, 360, 361, 362]; (2) Leucocytes—bone-marrow stem cell derivatives comprising six groups (monocyte-macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells, granulocytes, natural killer cells, and lymphocytes—where lymphocytes alone mediate adaptive immunity while the other five belong to innate immunity)[cite: 362, 363]; (3) Lymphoid organs—central (bone marrow and thymus, which matures T lymphocytes and shrinks with age) and peripheral (tonsils, gut/genital/bronchial/skin-associated lymphoid tissues, lymph nodes, and the spleen, whose white pulp holds B/T lymphocytes and red pulp holds erythrocytes; removing the spleen in children risks life-threatening septicaemia)[cite: 363, 364]; and (4) Mononuclear phagocyte system—blood monocytes and tissue macrophages that phagocytose, process, and present antigens to lymphocytes[cite: 364]. Five key properties govern immune responses: specificity, memory (faster, stronger secondary responses), self-recognition, self-limitation (shutting down once the antigen is cleared to prevent tissue injury), and specialization (tailored reactions to different pathogens)[cite: 364, 365].

content.heading: Types of Immunity, Antigens, Haptens, and MHC
content.body: Immunity divides into natural (innate) immunity—nonspecific first-line defence present at birth—and acquired (adaptive) immunity developed after exposure[cite: 366]. Acquired specific immunity is either Active or Passive[cite: 365, 366]. Natural active immunity follows clinical or subclinical infection (e.g., chickenpox, measles, mumps), develops slowly over weeks, and lasts long-term or for life[cite: 365]. Artificial active immunity follows vaccines or toxoids, develops slowly, and lasts several years with booster doses[cite: 365]. Natural passive immunity transfers maternal immunoglobulins across the placenta or in colostrum, giving immediate temporary protection for several months[cite: 365]. Artificial passive immunity injects preformed serum antibodies (pooled gamma-globulins), offering immediate protection for several weeks without creating memory cells[cite: 365, 367]. An antigen (immunogen)—typically protein, though large polysaccharides, lipoproteins, or nucleic acids can act as antigens—binds specific antibodies and triggers an immune response[cite: 367]. Haptens (such as dust, animal danders, drugs, and industrial chemicals) are harmless low-molecular-weight substances that become immunogenic only when bound to a carrier molecule, prompting three antibodies (against the hapten alone, the carrier alone, and the hapten-carrier complex) and underlying many allergies[cite: 368]. Self-recognition relies on Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) genes: Class I MHC proteins (human leucocyte antigens, HLAs) sit on almost all host cells and are unique to each person except identical twins (anything lacking HLA is recognized as nonself), whereas Class II MHC molecules reside mainly on immune cells and can be induced on other cells by antiviral interferons[cite: 369].

content.heading: Humoral vs. Cell-Mediated Immunity and Antigen-Antibody Interactions
content.body: Humoral immunity is antibody-mediated adaptive immunity driven by activated B lymphocytes differentiating into plasma cells that secrete five immunoglobulin classes—IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE (each composed of two light and two heavy polypeptide chains, differentiated by heavy-chain structure)—to produce immediate responses against extracellular bacteria, viruses, respiratory/GI pathogens, and exotoxins (e.g., anaphylaxis, atopy, transfusion reactions)[cite: 369, 371]. Cell-mediated immunity produces delayed responses mediated by T lymphocytes, macrophages, and natural killer (NK) cells against intracellular pathogens (viruses, Mycobacterium), fungi, tumour cells, transplanted grafts, and contact hypersensitivity[cite: 369, 370, 371]. T lymphocytes include T-cytotoxic cells (destroying target membranes via cytolytic substances), memory T cells, and immunoregulatory T-helper (CD4) and T-suppressor (CD8) cells—loss of T-suppressor balance drives autoimmune overactivity, while HIV destroys CD4 T-helper cells, predisposing patients to opportunistic infections and malignancies[cite: 370]. Large granular NK cells kill virus-infected cells, tumours, and grafts without prior sensitization[cite: 370]. Over 60 cytokines—lymphokines from lymphocytes and monokines from monocytes/macrophages, regulated by kinases (destroying cytokines) and kinase inhibitors (preserving cytokines)—include interleukins, colony-stimulating factors, and antiviral interferons, while activated macrophages release cytokines and tissue-damaging lysosomal enzymes[cite: 370, 371]. Antigen-antibody interactions eliminate antigens via five mechanisms: precipitation (insoluble lattices from soluble antigens), agglutination (clumping particulate antigens like RBCs), opsonization (coating bacteria with IgG and complement C3b for phagocytes), lysis (complement-mediated membrane rupture), and neutralization (inactivating bacterial toxins for phagocytic clearance)[cite: 371].

inTextQuestions.question: Which characteristic of an infectious agent specifically refers to its ability to cause disease, as opposed to growing/multiplying or entering tissues?
inTextQuestions.answer: Pathogenicity (whereas virulence is the ability to grow and multiply, and invasiveness is the ability to enter tissue)[cite: 333].

inTextQuestions.question: Why might an older adult with a serious infection fail to develop a fever, and what alternative clinical signs should a nurse watch for?
inTextQuestions.answer: Older adults have a lower baseline core body temperature and decreased immune responses, so fever may be absent; nurses should watch closely for cognitive and behavioural changes as signs of infection[cite: 335].

inTextQuestions.question: What is the role of epidermal Langerhans' cells in skin immunity, and what happens if they are depleted?
inTextQuestions.answer: Langerhans' cells form part of skin-associated lymphoid tissue in the epidermis; when depleted, the skin can neither initiate an immune response nor support a skin-localized delayed hypersensitivity reaction[cite: 359].

inTextQuestions.question: Why does artificial passive immunity (such as pooled gamma-globulin injection) provide immediate yet only short-lived protection?
inTextQuestions.answer: Because the host receives preformed antibodies rather than synthesizing them, yielding immediate defence but no memory cells for long-term protection[cite: 365, 367].

saqs.question: Define infection, list its three main types, and name the four stages through which all infections progress.
saqs.answer: Infection is the invasion of the body by a disease-causing microorganism (pathogen) with a resultant host response when host defences are overwhelmed[cite: 327]. Its three types are communicable diseases, nosocomial infections (healthcare-acquired), and opportunistic infections (affecting immunocompromised hosts)[cite: 328]. The four stages are incubation, prodromal, illness, and convalescence[cite: 329].

saqs.question: List the sequential links in the cycle of infection and give one nursing intervention used to break each of the following links: (a) agent-to-reservoir, (b) portal of exit-to-transmission, and (c) susceptible host-to-agent.
saqs.answer: The links are infectious agent, reservoir of infection, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host, and infection[cite: 329, 332]. Interventions: (a) cleansing, disinfection, and sterilization[cite: 333]; (b) hand hygiene, medical/surgical asepsis, proper disposal of contaminated items, and wearing gloves, masks, and goggles[cite: 333]; (c) good nutrition, immunization, exercise, adequate sleep/rest, and maintaining an intact immune system[cite: 334].

saqs.question: Explain how bacteria develop antibiotic resistance and state four factors that promote drug-resistant organisms.
saqs.answer: Bacteria adapt genetically (via mutation or acquiring new DNA) and biochemically (by producing enzymes that deactivate drugs), altering drug target sites so antibiotics cannot bind or enter[cite: 334]. Four promoting factors are: prescribing antibiotics for viral infections, succumbing to patient pressure for unnecessary antibiotics, using incomplete or inadequate drug regimens (or patients skipping/not finishing doses), and using broad-spectrum or combination agents when first-line drugs are appropriate[cite: 334].

saqs.question: Outline the three main functions of the immune system along with the maladaptive hyper- and hypo-responses associated with each.
saqs.answer: 1. Defence (destroying viruses, bacteria, fungi): hyper-response causes allergic disorders, and hypo-response causes immunodeficiency disorders[cite: 368]. 2. Homeostasis (removing damaged cells): hyper-response causes autoimmune diseases[cite: 368]. 3. Surveillance (removing mutated cells): hypo-response leads to malignant diseases[cite: 368].

saqs.question: Compare humoral immunity and cell-mediated immunity across cells involved, products, reaction speed, protective targets, and clinical examples.
saqs.answer: Humoral immunity involves B lymphocytes producing antibodies for immediate protection against extracellular bacteria, viruses, respiratory/GI pathogens, and exotoxins (e.g., anaphylactic shock, atopic diseases, transfusion reactions)[cite: 371]. Cell-mediated immunity involves T lymphocytes and macrophages producing sensitized T cells and lymphokines for delayed protection against intracellular viruses, fungi, and tumour cells (e.g., tuberculosis, fungal infections, contact dermatitis, graft rejection, cancer cell destruction)[cite: 371]. Both generate memory cells[cite: 371].
